claims.text: Initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles form a uniform solid solution.
Nanoscale chemical inhomogeneities, especially surface and subsurface segregation, govern premelting and melting behavior.
Local segregation lowers the energy barrier for atomic disordering.
The reduced barrier facilitates heterogeneous nucleation of a quasi-liquid layer.
Rapid quenching freezes a relatively uniform chemical distribution.
Slow cooling permits moderate chemical demixing.
Localized chemical demixing occurs at nanoparticle surfaces and grain boundaries.
Local compositional fluctuations decrease local cohesive energy.
Reduced local cohesive energy promotes early surface atomic mobility and disorder.
Chemical heterogeneity creates preferential sites for initiation of a quasi-liquid layer.
The quasi-liquid layer spreads and leads to complete melting.
Slow-cooled, measurably segregated nanoparticles will begin premelting at a lower temperature than rapidly quenched, more homogeneous nanoparticles.
Slow-cooled nanoparticles will exhibit a broader melting-transition temperature interval than rapidly quenched nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism is limited to the studied nanoparticle size range and temperatures near premelting and melting.
The mechanism may not apply to significantly larger particles, other alloy compositions, or systems dominated by external constraints.
Failure to observe either a significantly lower premelting onset in slow-cooled particles or a spatial correlation between segregation and quasi-liquid-layer initiation would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field characterizes the nanoparticles generally as a uniform solid solution, whereas the slow-cooled experimental population is defined as chemically demixed before heating. The intended timing and scope of the claimed uniform initial state are therefore inconsistent or insufficiently distinguished between the two cohorts.
